title: Y-D-A
carry: to know is to be close

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ch-N-N: chen, grace, the favor Noah found, given when nothing is owed. Today, a root about knowing.

A doctor can know your chart cover to cover and still not know you. A neighbor of many years can know your name, your car and your trash day, and nothing else. English uses one verb for all of it. Hebrew has a verb for knowing too, and in the Bible it keeps turning up where English would reach for a warmer word. A garden. A marriage. A name spoken by God. Three letters, yud, dalet, ayin: Y-D-A. And a simple question: what does it take to really know someone?
screen: `THE CHART, NOT THE PERSON.` → `ONE VERB IN ENGLISH.` → `Y-D-A: TO KNOW.`

segments.voice: Y-D-A gives yada, to know, and da'at, knowledge. Turn it four ways. First, the garden. In the middle of Eden stands "the tree of the knowledge of good and evil." Knowledge there is da'at, and in the story it isn't something you look up. You take it in, eat it, carry it inside you. Second, the marriage. Two chapters later: "And the man knew Eve his wife." Yada, for the closest two people can be. In the Bible's Hebrew, knowing can mean intimacy. Third, the name. Moses asks to be shown God's ways, and the answer comes: "thou hast found grace in My sight, and I know thee by name." Grace, yesterday's word, sits right beside knowing. To be known by name is to be held close, not filed away. Fourth, the hope. Jeremiah describes a day when no one will need to teach a neighbor about God, "for they shall all know Me, from the least of them unto the greatest of them." Not know about. Know. Some Jewish teachers read that as a relationship more than a fact, the way you know a friend's laugh across a crowded room. So the root always asks: arm's length, or up close? The neighbor who knows your trash day has information. The friend who can tell why you're quiet today has da'at.
screen: `THE GARDEN: DA'AT, KNOWLEDGE.` · `THE MARRIAGE: THE MAN KNEW EVE.` · `THE NAME: I KNOW THEE BY NAME.` · `THE HOPE: THEY SHALL ALL KNOW ME.` · then, large: `יָדַע`

segments.voice: Bring one person to mind, someone you see often but know only at arm's length: a coworker, a cousin, the person behind the counter. Notice what you know, a name, a habit, and then what you don't: what makes them laugh, who they miss, how their week has really gone. Let one real question for them take shape, and if you pray, bring their name with you into the quiet.
Y-D-A. Yud, dalet, ayin: the root of yada, to know, and da'at, knowledge, where knowing can mean closeness. Today's word.
Your line: to know is to be close. In the Bible's Hebrew, knowing was never only facts. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some Jewish teachers note that the Hebrew verb yada, to know, is used in the Bible for intimacy and relationship as well as for facts, and da'at, knowledge, is a word that recurs in Jewish prayer and study.
